case_study_insert.main_stem: Marlstone Roof Tiles (MRT) is a cooperative in the clay building products manufacturing sector, producing interlocking clay roof tiles and ridge pieces for housing developments, with a workforce of 48. Founded in 2011 by Martin Doyle, MRT operates a flat structure with democratic leadership and is owned by its 30 member workers. It plans to invest $950,000 in a new automated extrusion and kiln line for large-format tiles, financed by a $600,000 member share issue and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $342,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.60 a unit and a selling price of $7.60, and produces 171,000 units a year. MRT faces a 9% absenteeism rate on the kiln shift and labour turnover of 16%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — Q3 2025: A survey of 380 builders' merchants across four regions found that 57% expect large-format tile demand to grow, 46% would stock locally fired tiles at a 5% price premium and 38% currently import from overseas suppliers. Complaints about tile breakage in transit fell from 34 to 19 per month after the packaging change; average delivery lead time is 4.1 days. 11 of 48 workers have not completed kiln safety certification; the off-the-job kiln course at the construction college costs $820 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Marlstone Roof Tiles as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.00% to 5.75%, the fifth rise this year. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.6% from $12.80 to $13.52 per hour from April 2026. (3) Gas and electricity costs have risen 32.0% year-on-year following the pipeline outage, and input-cost inflation in construction materials is running at 8.3%, while housing starts grew 1.9% in the same period.

questions.question_text: MRT plans to finance part of its extrusion and kiln line with a $600,000 member share issue. Explain two advantages for MRT of the member share issue instead of a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A member share issue brings in $600,000 with no interest and no fixed repayment schedule, so MRT's flat, democratic co-op structure is not strained by servicing debt while gas and electricity costs are up 32.0%. Members who buy shares have a direct stake in the success of the large-format tile line, strengthening commitment and reducing the 16% labour turnover that fixed interest payments would silently undermine.

Point 2: Unlike a bank loan, a member share issue cannot be secured against the factory, the kilns or Martin Doyle's personal assets, and no lender can seize equipment if a housing-cycle downturn cuts orders. Because MRT is owned by its 30 member workers, decisions about dividend-style profit distributions remain with the membership, preserving democratic control and the social mission of local employment — whereas a bank would impose covenants and could force cost-cutting during the vulnerable first year of the new line.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Marlstone Roof Tiles and its extrusion and kiln expansion.

questions.question_text: MRT is launching its large-format tile for housing developments. Consider advertising in regional construction magazines, exhibiting at the National Housing and Construction Expo, or sponsoring show homes on flagship housing sites. Which should MRT choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Regional construction magazines: Quarter-page adverts in titles such as Regional Builder and Merchant Monthly, costing only a few thousand dollars per issue, reach merchants and specifiers directly, and suit MRT's story that 46% of surveyed merchants would stock locally fired tiles at a 5% premium. Print builds quiet credibility with traditional specifiers over time, but response is slow, unmeasurable, and the 38% of merchants currently importing overseas tiles may never read the ads.

National Housing and Construction Expo: A stand at the expo, absorbing a sizeable slice of the $950,000 line's budget, puts MRT face-to-face with the 57% of merchants expecting large-format demand to grow, with tiles stacked and handling demonstrations running all week. It is MRT's best shot at signing framework deals with the big housing developers whose orders fill a 171,000-unit year, but it consumes member-leaders' time and yields most enquiries from already-decided buyers.

Show-home sponsorship: Branding MRT tiles in flagship show homes on regional housing sites puts the product in front of thousands of buyers and developers who specify by sight. It is emotionally powerful but passive: MRT cannot easily trace orders back to the show homes, and exposure ends when the development sells out.

Recommendation: MRT should choose the National Housing and Construction Expo. For a capital-goods tile manufacturer, the buying decision sits with a small number of merchants and developer specifiers, and the expo is the one venue where all of them gather; a single framework agreement could cover the $950,000 line's first-year throughput. Regional magazines are rejected as too slow and unmeasurable for a launch window; show-home sponsorship is rejected as untrackable and developer-dependent. MRT should keep a modest magazine presence as a reminder channel after the expo.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MRT with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MRT with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazines and show-home sponsorship are rejected as the lead channel.

questions.question_text: MRT operates a flat structure with democratic leadership and a 9% absenteeism rate on the kiln shift. Explain two benefits for MRT of democratic leadership for its member-owned workforce.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership treats the 48 workers — 30 of them member owners — as partners in decisions on firing schedules, shift patterns and safety, satisfying esteem and belonging needs and building genuine commitment to the co-op. Members consulted on the kiln roster are more likely to attend consistently, directly attacking the 9% absenteeism rate on the kiln shift and protecting continuous firing, which wastes days of energy if interrupted.

Point 2: Involvement releases practical knowledge held only by people at the kiln mouth and the extrusion line — for instance on clay moisture, extrusion speed and the causes of tile breakage in transit. Their suggestions already cut breakage complaints from 34 to 19 per month after the packaging change; democratic channels keep that intelligence flowing, improve the 16% labour turnover position, and align member incentives around the success of the $950,000 large-format line. Democratic review of kiln loading also keeps the 30 member owners accountable to one another, so the 9% absenteeism rate is treated as a collective responsibility discussed openly rather than a private failing, deterring slippage before it becomes costly firing delays.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MRT's absenteeism, complaints and expansion.

questions.question_text: MRT is growing and must decide how to organise the business. Consider introducing a two-tier hierarchy with team leaders over three kiln crews, or keeping the flat structure with enlarged teams. Which should MRT choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Two-tier hierarchy with team leaders: Naming three team leaders (one per kiln crew plus one for extrusion) would reduce each co-op member's span of control, create clear promotion routes for skilled members, and give Martin Doyle reliable daily reporting as the $950,000 automated line comes online. Fair discipline on safety and the 9% kiln-shift absenteeism would become easier. Drawbacks are added payroll cost for the leader allowances, an extra management layer that slows flat democratic decision-making, risk of resentment if members perceive bosses, and it partially dilutes the co-op ethos that makes MRT distinctive.

Keeping the flat structure with enlarged teams: Enlarging existing crews (adding a second firing shift) keeps democracy direct, preserves equality among members, avoids fixed salary inflation, and leverages the existing democratic meeting rhythm. However, 16-person teams strain communication, no one owns daily discipline, the 9% absenteeism problem can hide inside larger groups, and Martin Doyle becomes a bottleneck for every quality and safety decision as output heads toward 171,000 units.

Decision: MRT should introduce the two-tier hierarchy, selecting team leaders by member vote with a small fixed allowance rather than salary. This retains democratic legitimacy (leaders are elected, not imposed), gives the kiln roster the accountability it needs to hold absenteeism at bay, and scales MRT toward the large-format line without abandoning co-op principles. Keeping the purely flat structure is rejected because at 48 staff and rising output it has started to fail — Martin Doyle cannot personally monitor every firing — while unelected managerial layers are rejected as a betrayal of the membership model that keeps labour turnover survivable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two structural options with limited application to MRT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of hierarchy versus flat structure in the context of MRT.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of MRT with a well-justified decision covering cost, democracy, accountability and scale.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MRT's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $342,000 ÷ ($7.60 − $3.60) = $342,000 ÷ $4.00 = 85,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 85,500 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $7.60 − $3.60 = $4.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MRT's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 85,500-unit break-even output with the current output of 171,000 units to confirm the tile line is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 85,500 units, before approving phase two of the kiln investment.
2. A contribution per unit of $4.00 lets MRT model the 5% premium that 46% of merchants say they will pay for locally fired tiles: a 5% price increase to $7.98 lifts contribution to $4.38, quantifying exactly how much headroom exists against the 32.0% energy-cost inflation now hitting the kilns.
3. Fixed costs of $342,000 combined with the $4.00 contribution helps managers test whether the $950,000 automated line, funded by a $600,000 member share issue and $350,000 retained profit, can generate the operating cash surplus needed for future reinvestment and member dividends.
4. Unit cost data ($342,000 ÷ 171,000 units + $3.60 = $5.60) lets managers benchmark each quarter, target the breakage rate (complaints down from 34 to 19 per month) for further reduction, negotiate clay and gas supply contracts, and monitor labour productivity of about 3,563 units per worker (171,000 ÷ 48) to plan rosters around the 9% kiln-shift absenteeism.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 85,500 units ($342,000 ÷ $4.00) | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.00 ($7.60 − $3.60) | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 85,500 units against 171,000-unit output; 5% local-premium modelling to $7.98 (contribution $4.38) against the 32.0% energy-cost spike; feasibility check for the $600,000 member share issue funding the $950,000 extrusion and kiln line; unit-cost benchmarking at $5.60, breakage tracking (complaints down from 34 to 19 per month) and about 3,563 units per worker labour productivity.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MRT's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MRT's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.55 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.73 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.98 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $260,000 inventories + $175,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $495,000; 2025 current assets = $215,000 + $190,000 + $105,000 = $510,000. 2024: $495,000 ÷ $320,000 = 1.55; 2025: $510,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.70. For the stricter measure, 2024: ($495,000 − $260,000) ÷ $320,000 = $235,000 ÷ $320,000 = 0.73; 2025: ($510,000 − $215,000) ÷ $300,000 = $295,000 ÷ $300,000 = 0.98.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved, though the acid test remains just below 1.00 and therefore still merits caution. The improvement was driven by quality of assets rather than asset growth: inventories fell from $260,000 to $215,000 as firing rhythm stabilised and breakage complaints dropped from 34 to 19 per month, and cash almost doubled from $60,000 to $105,000, giving MRT real headroom to service the $600,000 member share issue programme and approach the kiln upgrade. Current liabilities fell from $320,000 to $300,000, so the stronger coverage ratios are not borrowed. However, trade receivables crept up from $175,000 to $190,000, and the energy-cost spike of 32.0% means future cash generation could be squeezed even as headline liquidity improves.

Conclusion: MRT's financial position has improved. Liquidity strengthened on both measures, inventories fell, cash rose strongly and liabilities fell — a genuine, operational improvement. The remaining weakness is an acid test of 0.98, still short of $1 of liquid assets per $1 of short-term debt, so MRT should tighten merchant credit terms and negotiate milestone deposits from housebuilders before the full draw-down of the member share issue.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether MRT's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MRT of switching its kiln from gas to biomass and renewable energy.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Switching to biomass and renewable energy would shield MRT from the 32.0% gas-price spike now hitting the kilns and from future volatility, cutting the energy component of its $3.60 variable cost and protecting the $4.00 contribution. It also strengthens MRT's environmental story with the 46% of merchants willing to pay a 5% premium for locally fired tiles, and gives the co-op a genuine sustainability credential to market on packs and at the National Housing and Construction Expo.

Disadvantage: Kiln conversion is capital-intensive — burners, feed systems and drying controls would cost a significant capital sum on top of the $950,000 line — and biomass supply is less reliable than piped gas, with moisture content and ash handling creating new quality risks for tile colour consistency. Any firing interruption from fuel shortage would halt flat, continuous production and repeat the industry-wide quality failures that gas kilns avoid, and members would bear the risk of cost overruns through their share issue.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MRT's energy costs, contribution and co-op structure.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.6% minimum wage increase and the 32.0% rise in gas and electricity costs will affect MRT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise to 5.75%: MRT's funding mix is deliberately interest-light — a $600,000 member share issue and $350,000 retained profit, with no bank loan — so the direct pass-through of the base rate moving from 5.00% to 5.75% is limited to any short-term working-capital costs, which will be minimal. The real risk is indirect: merchants holding lower cash balances may delay tile orders, and housing developers may slow project starts.

Minimum wage increase of 5.6% to $13.52: MRT's 48 staff — 30 of them members paid at or near the minimum plus member surplus — face a wage bill up roughly 5.6%. At average earnings near $13.52 an hour for 2,080 hours, each worker adds about $1,490 a year, or around $71,500 across the workforce. For a co-op, though, members vote on how to absorb this, for instance via smaller member surplus distributions rather than cuts.

Gas and electricity cost inflation of 32.0%: Clay tiles need firing; energy is the largest single component of MRT's $3.60 variable cost, roughly $1.45 per unit (about 40%). A 32.0% rise adds about $0.46 per tile. Across 171,000 units that is roughly $79,000 a year, compressing contribution per unit from $4.00 toward $3.54, narrowing margin of safety, and directly threatening the return behind the $950,000 extrusion and kiln line.

Conclusion: The 32.0% rise in gas and electricity costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every unit fired, outweighs the wage rise (~$71,500) and swamps the interest-rate effect (minimal). Unlike wages, energy cannot be re-spread by improving attendance, and unlike the 1.9% growth in housing starts it cannot be forecast away. MRT should hedge biomass/dual-fuel contracts, press for a 5% local-premium price increase across its merchant base, and evaluate the biomass conversion in Q4 before the next member dividends are declared.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to MRT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MRT's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of MRT with a well-justified judgement that energy-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
